free_text.inst.v2.D8:
Half the page is empty. What reads well - nothing under it. What reads hard - nothing. Right now - nothing. Then a list. I have been handed better nonsense than this by better-dressed men.

It opens by calling me responsive and changeable, led by feeling. No. I was raised by a Prussian widow who said the word duty the way other mothers say darling, and I have never in my life done a thing because I felt like it. I stood in wet fields singing for boys with frostbite because it was the work. I lost my accent, my weight, my country and my name because it was the work. Changeable is what people call a woman who will not explain herself.

Then it says the hard parts are work and standing, and that it is unusually negative about recognition for what I did. That is the one place it tells you to test it, so test it there: the Medal of Freedom, the Legion of Honour, a Tony, my face on the wall of every projection booth from Los Angeles to Tel Aviv. Whatever was taken from me, it was not recognition. My own country withheld it - they spat at me in Dusseldorf in 1960 and called me traitor - but I did not need Germany's permission and I did not wait for it. It also says courage reads hard. I went to the front. Let it explain that one to the men of the Third Army.

Where it is right: property, and time away from home. I owned nothing. Trunks, hotels, a rented flat on the Avenue Montaigne, and a bed I did not leave for the last thirteen years. It says brothers and sisters read hard - I had a sister; I found her at Belsen in 1945 and I have said since that I was an only child; make of that what you like. It says my mother reads hard, and there it lies. She was the one steady thing in ninety years, and I got her into the ground in a ruined city in November 1945 with a wooden box and no priest.

Children, it says, read hard. I had one daughter. She was there for all of it, which is more than I can say for anybody else on the list.

It admits itself that most of this would fit most people. That is the only honest sentence on the page. No, I would not pay for it.

notes: Answered in persona as Marlene Dietrich (b. 27 Dec 1901 Berlin-Schoneberg, d. 6 May 1992 Paris, aged 90, renal failure), having read the prepared reading first. The reading is mostly empty scaffolding; its substantive claims are a temperament line, a house-by-house good/hard/mixed list, and a flag that it is 'unusually negative about recognition for your work, land and property and work and standing'. Where it conflicted with the documented life, the life won. Specific conflicts and what I did: (1) temperament - it calls her 'responsive and changeable, guided a good deal by feeling'; the record is Prussian discipline, control and duty, so B1 went to opt2 (wants to be seen and respected, generous, proud, does not take correction easily) and A30 to outspoken/bold/practical/sociable, not the feeling-led profile. (2) recognition, work and standing - the reading's most distinctive claim is that these read hard; the life is the Medal of Freedom (1947), the Legion d'honneur (Chevalier 1950 to Commandeur 1989), a special Tony (1968) and world fame, so A19=about_right, C5=opt1 and C6=opt1 at confidence 4, all against the reading. (3) courage and siblings - it calls both hard; courage is flatly wrong (front-line tours under fire, refusing Goebbels, US citizenship in 1939), the sister is right (Elisabeth, found at Bergen in 1945, afterwards disowned; A13=conflicted), so the item was split rather than accepted whole. (4) mother - it reads the 4th hard; Josephine was the one steady attachment of her life, so A12=close. Where the reading and the life agreed I felt real pull and kept the confidence deliberately moderate rather than inflated: C4 (land and property, opt2 at 3) and the 12th-house 'time away from home' line are both genuinely true of a woman who owned no house and died in a rented Paris flat, and D2 credits 'houses' for exactly that - but 3, not 5, because the agreement is not independent of having just read the claim. Contamination is also visible in D8, which argues line by line with the plain-English page and quotes its own 'test it there' back at it. A24=widowed (Rudolf Sieber, married 17 May 1923, died 24 June 1976; never divorced). A36 (since mid-2023) is anachronistic for someone who died in 1992 and was answered 'same' as the least distorting response. Two dates are approximate: the father's death is given as 1907 (some sources 1908) and the 1973 Washington stage fall has no month recorded here. Cervical illness and cirrhosis appear in some biographies but were left out of A6 as insufficiently certain; A6 keeps only the well-documented legs/circulation, nerves-sleep-alcohol dependence, and the kidney failure that killed her.
